A sharp knife is safer than a dull one. Here's how to keep it that way.

  1. Hone first. Hold the rod vertically, knife at 20° angle, draw down each side 5-10 times.
  2. Test. Slice paper. If it drags, move to the stone.
  3. Soak your whetstone in water for 10 minutes.
  4. Sharpen at 20°. Push the blade across the stone like you're slicing a thin layer off the top. 10 passes per side.
  5. Flip and repeat. Then do 5 lighter passes per side.
  6. Wipe clean, dry, and hone again.

Don't use a pull-through sharpener on good knives. It chews the edge.

Crushed eggshells add calcium and keep the pile sweet. Here's the quick version—user_name.

Eggshell Compost Boost

Balance greens and browns, keep pests out, feed the soil.

cached Updated for spring

Why it works

Shells are ~95% calcium carbonate—the same stuff garden lime is made of. Worms and microbes break it down slowly. Plants use the calcium for strong cell walls, and it nudges pH up a touch if your soil runs sour.

How to do it

  1. Rinse shells so they don't smell like yesterday's omelet.
  2. Dry them on the counter, then crush to powder or small bits. Powder works faster.
  3. Mix into the pile. Ratio: about 1 cup crushed shells per 4 cups scraps.
  4. Turn the pile monthly. Shells won't fully vanish for a year—that's fine.

Pest note

Whole shells attract rodents and flies. Crushing is non-negotiable. If you see critters, bury shells deeper in the center.

Blender shortcut

Pulse dry shells in a blender until sandy. Wear earplugs. It's loud.

Can I skip rinsing?

Yes, but you'll smell it by Tuesday. A quick swish is worth it.

Good sign: pile hits 130–150°F and smells earthy, not rotten.

Umi

That's the whole shell game. Happy composting.

Deglazing a Pan for Quick Sauce

Turn the browned bits stuck to the pan into a fast pan sauce. Works with stainless, cast iron, or carbon steel — not nonstick.

Why it works: The brown bits (fond) are concentrated flavor. A splash of liquid lifts them and becomes sauce in under a minute.

  1. Finish searing. Move meat to a plate. Leave the pan on medium heat — fond should be deep brown, not black.
  2. Pour in liquid. Use ¼–½ cup wine, broth, or even water. It will hiss and steam.
  3. Scrape. Use a wooden spoon or spatula to loosen every brown speck. Simmer 1–2 minutes until reduced by half.
  4. Swirl in cold butter. Off heat, add 1–2 tablespoons cold butter, swirling until glossy. Taste and season.
What liquid should I use?
  • Wine — dry white or red; let the alcohol cook off.
  • Broth — chicken or beef; milder.
  • Vinegar + water — 1 tablespoon vinegar to ½ cup water for a bright kick.
  • Water — in a pinch, works fine.

If fond is black: It's bitter. Wipe the pan, add fresh fat, and start over — no sauce will fix burnt bits.

Add a minced shallot or garlic clove after scraping for extra depth. A pat of butter at the end makes it restaurant-silky.

Snake Plant Watering & Care

Also called mother-in-law's tongue. Tough, but it has one fatal weakness: too much water.

Golden rule: Let the soil dry completely before watering. In summer that's every 2–3 weeks; in winter, every 4–6 weeks.

How to water properly
  1. Check soil with a finger or moisture meter. Bone dry? Water.
  2. Water until it runs out the drainage hole. Never let it sit in a saucer of water.
  3. Empty the saucer after 10 minutes.
Light & placement

Bright, indirect light is ideal. It tolerates low light but grows slower. Avoid direct afternoon sun — leaves can scorch.

Brown tips or mushy base?
  • Brown tips: Usually tap water minerals or inconsistent watering. Switch to filtered water.
  • Mushy base: Root rot from overwatering. Remove from pot, trim mushy roots, repot in dry cactus mix, and wait a week before watering.

Feed once in spring and once in summer with diluted houseplant fertilizer. Otherwise, ignore it — it prefers neglect.

Cold Brew Coffee at Home

Smooth, low-acid, and forgiving. No fancy gear needed.

Basic ratio: 1 part coarse coffee to 4 parts cold water by weight. For a 1-quart jar: 100g coffee + 400g water.

  1. Grind coarse. Like sea salt. A burr grinder is best, but a blade grinder pulsed works in a pinch.
  2. Combine. Stir coffee and water in a jar. Cover.
  3. Steep 12–18 hours at room temperature (or 24 hours in the fridge for a cleaner taste).
  4. Strain. Pour through a fine-mesh sieve lined with a coffee filter or cheesecloth. Discard grounds.
  5. Dilute to taste. The concentrate is strong. Mix 1:1 with water or milk.
Cold brew vs. iced coffee

Iced coffee is brewed hot and chilled — brighter, more acidic. Cold brew steeps cold — smoother, less acidic, higher caffeine per ounce.

Too weak? Next batch, use more coffee or steep longer. Don't over-dilute — taste before adding water.

Store concentrate in the fridge up to 2 weeks. Shake before serving.

Dishwasher Filter Cleaning

A dirty filter makes dishes gritty and the whole kitchen smell like a wet dog. Most manufacturers say clean it monthly.

Time: 5–10 minutes. No tools needed for most models.

  1. Find the filter. Open the door and look at the bottom. It's usually a cylindrical mesh screen in the center or back corner.
  2. Remove it. Twist counterclockwise or lift straight up. Some have two parts — a coarse and a fine filter.
  3. Rinse under hot water. Use a soft brush (old toothbrush works) to scrub away food bits and grease.
  4. Soak if greasy. 10 minutes in hot water + a drop of dish soap.
  5. Reinstall. Twist until it locks. Run a rinse cycle to check.
Still smells? Try this.

Place a cup of white vinegar on the top rack and run a hot water cycle. Then sprinkle baking soda on the bottom and run a short cycle. This kills odor-causing bacteria.

Never use bleach in a stainless steel dishwasher — it can corrode the tub.

Also check the spray arms for clogged holes. A toothpick clears them.

Hanging Pictures Right

No more crooked frames or Swiss-cheese walls.

Height rule: Center of the art at 57–60 inches from the floor — average eye level. Over furniture, leave 6–8 inches between the frame bottom and the tabletop or sofa back.

Which hanger for my wall?

  • Drywall, heavy frame: Use a drywall anchor and screw. Toggle bolts for really heavy pieces.
  • Plaster or lath: Drill a pilot hole to avoid cracks. Use a screw with an anchor.
  • Brick or concrete: Masonry bit + plastic anchor + screw.
How to hang straight every time
  1. Flip the frame over. Stretch a piece of painter's tape across the back, sticky side out.
  2. Poke the tape where the hanger hooks sit. That marks the exact spots on the wall.
  3. Stick the tape on the wall, level it, and nail through the marks.

Adhesive strips can fail in humid rooms or on textured walls. For anything over 5 lbs, use a nail or anchor.

Use two hooks for wide or heavy frames to keep them from tilting.

Silence a Squeaky Door

That chirp is metal rubbing metal. Lubricant fixes it in 2 minutes.

Best lubes: White lithium grease, silicone spray, or petroleum jelly. Avoid cooking oil — it gets gummy.

  1. Wipe the hinge. Dirt and old grease cause friction. A rag and a little rubbing alcohol work.
  2. Lift the pin. Tap the hinge pin up from below with a screwdriver and hammer. Don't remove it completely — just lift it an inch.
  3. Lubricate. Apply a dab of grease to the pin and inside the hinge knuckles.
  4. Tap it back. Gently hammer the pin down until it's flush.
  5. Swing the door back and forth a few times to spread the lube.
Still squeaks?

The hinge might be worn. If the door sags or the pin wiggles, replace the hinge — they're cheap and sold at any hardware store.

WD-40 is a solvent, not a lubricant. It'll silence the squeak for a week, then it comes back worse. Use actual grease.

Do all three hinges while you're at it. Future you will thank you.

Fitted Sheet Folding Trick

No more crumpled ball.

Here's the easy way to fold a fitted sheet.

  1. Hold the sheet inside out, with the elastic edges facing you.
  2. Put your hands into two adjacent corners (like mittens).
  3. Fold one corner over the other, tucking it in. Repeat with the remaining two corners so all four are stacked.
  4. Lay the sheet on a flat surface, smooth it out.
  5. Fold in half lengthwise, then fold the elastic edges inward to make a rectangle.
  6. Fold in half again or thirds to desired size.

The key is to tuck the corners into each other—no elastic snapping.

Keep your grind fresh.

No scrubbing needed.

Loosen stuck-on food with steam.

  3. Let sit for 5 minutes (don't open yet).

  5. For stubborn spots, repeat or use a paste of baking soda and water.

Leave the door open afterward to dry and prevent odors.

Drain Unclogging Basics

Try these before calling a plumber.

Start with the gentlest method.

  1. Boiling water: Pour a kettle of boiling water down the drain in stages. Works for grease and soap scum.
  2. Baking soda + vinegar: Pour 1/2 cup baking soda, then 1/2 cup vinegar. Cover with a plug. Wait 15 minutes, then flush with hot water.
  3. Plunger: Use a cup plunger for sinks, flange plunger for toilets. Seal the drain and plunge vigorously.
  4. Drain snake: Feed a manual snake into the drain, crank to break up clogs.

Avoid chemical drain cleaners—they can damage pipes.

Fix a Dripping Kitchen Faucet

Most drips come from a worn washer, O‑ring, or cartridge. Turn off the water supply and relieve pressure before opening the handle.

Step‑by‑step
  1. Shut off the hot and cold valves under the sink (or main). Open the faucet to drain.
  2. Plug the drain so small parts don’t vanish.
  3. Pry off the handle cap, unscrew the set screw, lift off the handle.
  4. Remove the retaining nut, pull out the cartridge or stem.
  5. Inspect O‑rings and washers. Replace any that are cracked or flattened. Match parts exactly—take them to the store.
  6. Reassemble in reverse order. Hand‑tighten the nut, then a quarter turn with a wrench.
  7. Turn water back on slowly. Check for leaks. Run hot and cold to flush.

If the drip continues, the valve seat may be scratched. A seat‑grinding tool can smooth it, or replace the faucet.

Clean Your Coffee Maker

Oils and mineral scale build up, making coffee bitter and slow. A monthly vinegar run keeps it tasting fresh.

Step‑by‑step

  2. Place a filter in the basket and start a brew cycle. Stop halfway and let it sit for 30 minutes.
  3. Finish the cycle, then discard the vinegar solution.
  4. Run two or three full cycles with plain water to rinse.
  5. Wash the carafe, basket, and lid with warm soapy water. Rinse well.
  6. Wipe the exterior with a damp cloth. Don’t immerse the base.

Stop a Running Toilet

A running toilet wastes water and money. The culprit is usually the flapper, fill valve, or float. Here’s how to diagnose and fix it.

Common fixes
  • Flapper: If water runs intermittently, the flapper may not seal. Turn off water, empty tank, and replace the flapper (cheap and easy).
  • Float: If water runs constantly, the float may be set too high. Adjust the screw or clip so the water stops about an inch below the overflow tube.
  • Fill valve: If the tank won’t fill or runs forever, the fill valve may be faulty. Replace it—it’s a bit more involved but doable.
  • Chain: Make sure the chain isn’t caught under the flapper or too long.

Always turn off the water supply and flush before working. Keep a towel handy.

Fruit flies are drawn to fermenting smells. The vinegar mimics that, and the soap makes them drown instead of float.

If your dishes come out gritty or the machine smells, the filter is the usual suspect. Here's the quick routine.

  4. For greasy film, soak in hot water with a drop of dish soap for 5 minutes, then scrub again.
  5. Check the sump area for glass shards or bones. Wipe with a damp cloth.
  6. Reassemble and run a hot cycle with a cup of white vinegar in the top rack.

Once a month is plenty. If you have hard water, check the filter every two weeks—minerals clog it faster.

  4. For a fill valve: same shutoff, then replace the whole fill valve assembly (about $15). Follow the package instructions—it's a 20-minute job.
  5. Turn water back on, let the tank fill, and check for leaks.

If the tank is cracked or the bolts are rusted solid, call a plumber. Some things aren't worth the knuckle skin.

Full pressure at the top should produce full flow at the bottom within a few seconds. If it dribbles, there's still a plug above the elbow.

  2. Close the door and try to pull it out.
  3. Repeat every twelve inches around the frame.

Slight drag is good. Slides out freely means a gap at that spot.

Common culprits: crumbs on the gasket, a worn hinge letting the door sag, or a bulging item pushing the shelf out.
Fixes in order of effort
  1. Wipe the gasket with warm soapy water and dry it. Corners hide the most gunk.
  2. Straighten a pinched gasket by pressing it back into its channel.
  3. Tighten the hinge screws or shim the hinge plate if the door sags.

Pull the nib with pliers, flip or replace it, and drop ink on the inner wick. Messy, but a last resort that works.

  • Apply a drop of lubricant (WD-40, silicone spray, or even cooking oil) to the top of each hinge pin.
  • Open and close the door a few times to work it in.
  • Wipe excess to avoid drips.

No lubricant? Rub a pencil lead on the pin.

instances.html:
Remove Ballpoint Ink from Fabric

Props: none

Act fast—ink sets with heat.

  1. Place a clean white cloth under the stain.
  2. Dab (don't rub) with rubbing alcohol or hairspray on a cotton ball.
  3. As ink transfers, move to a clean part of the cloth.
  4. Repeat until no more ink lifts.
  5. Launder as usual.

Test alcohol on a hidden spot first.

instances.title: Revive Wilted Lettuce
instances.html:
Revive Wilted Lettuce

Props: none

Don't toss it yet—lettuce just needs a drink.

  1. Cut off the root end and separate leaves.
  2. Fill a bowl with ice water.
  3. Soak leaves for 15–30 minutes.
  4. Dry in a salad spinner or pat with towels.

Crisp again in no time. Works for kale and herbs too.

Fix a Wobbly Table

Props: none

No more drinks sloshing. Here's how:

  • Turn the table upside down; check if leg screws are loose. Tighten them.
  • If legs are uneven, add felt pads to the short leg.
  • For a quick fix, fold a piece of paper and wedge it under the short leg.
  • Still wobbly? A thin slice of cork or a coin can work.

Level it once; enjoy stable meals forever.

Whiten Dingy White Sneakers

Bring back the bright:

  1. Remove laces; wash them separately.
  2. Mix baking soda and laundry detergent into a paste.
  3. Scrub shoes with an old toothbrush.
  4. Wipe with a damp cloth.
  5. For stubborn scuffs, use a magic eraser.
  6. Air dry—never in direct sun or dryer.

White again, like new.
